_note: Narration script for the Anaphylaxis module (CPP-003-AO v3.0). Generated as one take with the Lee voice; one paragraph per scene.

lines.head: Introduction
sentences: Anaphylaxis.
What every Ambulance Officer needs to know.

lines.head: What it is
sentences: Anaphylaxis is a potentially life threatening severe allergic reaction.
Treat it as a medical emergency that needs immediate treatment.
It can follow a mild or moderate reaction, so keep watching.

lines.head: The signs
sentences: Look for difficult or noisy breathing, swelling of the tongue, tightness in the throat, a hoarse voice or trouble talking.
Also a wheeze or persistent cough, and persistent dizziness or collapse.
In young children, they may be pale and floppy.

lines.head: When to give adrenaline
sentences: Give adrenaline when you suspect anaphylaxis and the patient has hypotension, severe bronchospasm, or severe breathing distress from airway swelling.
Any one of those is enough.

lines.head: Basic care
sentences: Lay the patient flat, unless their breathing is difficult.
Do not let them stand or walk.
Remove the trigger if you can, and request clinical support.

lines.head: The auto-injector
sentences: Follow the patient's anaphylaxis plan, if it is immediately available.
Use their prescribed adrenaline auto-injector as a priority.

lines.head: Using an EpiPen
sentences: Remove the blue cap, push the orange end firmly against the mid thigh until it clicks, and hold it there for ten seconds or more.
It can be given through clothing if required.
Then gently massage the site for ten seconds.

lines.head: No auto-injector
sentences: If there is no auto-injector, consult the E O C Clinician.
They may advise intramuscular adrenaline, ten micrograms per kilogram, with a single maximum dose of five hundred micrograms.
Further doses can be given if required.

lines.head: The dose
sentences: So a twenty kilogram child may be advised two hundred micrograms.
From fifty kilograms up, the dose is capped at five hundred micrograms.

lines.head: Asthma and transport
sentences: If a patient with known asthma and an allergy has sudden breathing difficulty, treat for anaphylaxis before any asthma medication.
Continue basic care, provide prompt transport, and notify the receiving facility.
Every allergy patient goes to a health facility, even if they seem to recover.

lines.head: Wrap-up
sentences: So: look for the signs, lay them flat, give adrenaline early, use the auto-injector first, and always transport.
Then try the adrenaline checker on this page.
